title: Read the day with Analytics
description: Understand what the dashboard totals mean, where they come from and how to inspect the underlying recordings.

chapters.title: A view of results already produced

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional shop manager asking how busy the entrance was yesterday. The Analytics page has counts and charts, but does opening it run a fresh analysis on all the video?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Analytics is a read-only view over recordings and results the processing services already produced. Changing filters asks for another view of that data; it doesn't rerun the analysis.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So a zero count isn't automatically proof that nobody entered?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Exactly. It might mean the relevant alert wasn't configured, no matching recording arrived, or the expected analysis didn't run. Read the numbers in the context of how they were produced.

chapters.title: Set the scope before reading totals

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Our manager only cares about the shop entrance, not the warehouse. What's the first useful action?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose the day, site and devices. Those controls scope the cards, charts and tables together. Available dates come from indexed recording dates, so the date picker itself reflects which days have data for the current context.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Then the cards answer different questions about the same selected day?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Yes. Recordings, connected devices, counted objects and time in regions represent different measurements. Don't treat recording volume as a count of people, or a cumulative region duration as the length of one particular visit.

chapters.title: Use charts to find the next question

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The entrance has a spike in the afternoon. How does the manager move from a big number to something inspectable?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Hourly charts show how activity is distributed across the day. The count chart can separate devices or alerts, and direction filters can narrow the view. Tables list the events behind the totals and link back to recordings.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: That's more useful than pointing at a chart and declaring the mystery solved.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Exactly. Use the chart to identify the period worth investigating, then review the underlying event and footage. Comparing recording volume can also help explain whether a change came from activity or from what cameras actually uploaded.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can everyone who sees a count change the alert behind it?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Results follow access to the relevant devices and sites. Editing alerts requires its own permission. A management link is navigation, not a new grant of access.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What's a sensible first check if the expected count is missing?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Confirm the selected day and devices, then check that recordings and the relevant analysis or alert results exist. The guide explains the deployment requirements. A dashboard can't invent results that were never generated, and it doesn't backfill them by being opened.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
